design_detail: Cross-sectional study of published trial reports (meta-research; not about drugs used outside medicine). From a cohort of 616 reports of randomized controlled trials published in December 2006 and indexed in PubMed by 22 March 2007 (found with the Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy and described in an earlier study, ref. 11), the authors selected the 205 two-arm parallel-group trials with a clearly identified primary outcome and, of these, the 72 with statistically non-significant results (P ≥ .05) for all primary outcomes. Two readers independently read title, abstract, main text and online appendices with a pretested standardized form, resolving disagreements by consensus or with a third reader, and classified 'spin' (reporting strategies, whatever their motive, that highlight a benefit of the experimental treatment despite a non-significant primary outcome, or distract the reader from that result) by section, strategy, extent and level, using a scheme the authors developed. Proportions with 95% CIs (pp. 2059–2060); the paper does not name the method, and the editors' recalculation reproduces them as exact (Clopper–Pearson) intervals.
can_establish: How often, in 72 reports of two-arm parallel-group trials published in December 2006 whose primary outcomes were not statistically significant, titles, abstracts and main texts presented the results in ways inconsistent with that primary result, and by which strategies.
cannot_establish: Whether the spin was deliberate or came from lack of knowledge, or whether it changed readers' or reviewers' interpretation (the authors say they cannot tell, p. 2063); how common spin is in trials with significant results, in other designs or years, or in drug research specifically; or any link with funding (not analysed).

sample.recruitment: Published reports in a cohort of randomized trials published in December 2006 and indexed in PubMed by 22 March 2007: 1735 citations, 879 full texts reviewed, 616 included (pp. 2059–2060; Figure, p. 2060).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: parallel-group RCTs with a clearly identified primary outcome (explicitly stated, in the sample size calculation, or in the primary objectives) and non-significant results (P ≥ .05) for all primary outcomes; where no formal test was reported the authors calculated the effect and its CI. Excluded: cost-effectiveness and diagnostic test accuracy reports, non-English reports, equivalence or noninferiority, crossover, cluster, factorial and split-body trials, trials with more than 2 groups, and phase 2 trials (p. 2059). Of the 616: 122 had no identified primary outcome, 100 were crossover, 93 multiple-group, 26 pilot studies, 16 split-body, 13 cluster, 10 brief communications or letters, 10 factorial, 10 noninferiority or equivalence trials, 5 phase 1, 3 phase 2, 1 sequential and 2 other (Figure, p. 2060). One reviewer screened full texts and classified primary results by significance (p. 2059).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (documents). The 72 reports: 69 (95.8%) in specialty journals and 3 (4.2%) in general medical journals; cardiology, obstetrics and gynaecology and surgery 9 each (12.5%), psychiatry or psychology 7 (9.7%), anaesthesia 5 (6.9%); primary outcome efficacy in 63 (87.5%), safety in 7 (9.7%); median sample size 84 (IQR 46–206; range 4–6848); median 2007 impact factor 2.9; experimental treatment a drug in 37 (51.4%); comparator a placebo in 19 (26.4%); funding for-profit in 16 (22.2%), for-profit and non-profit in 8 (11.1%), non-profit in 19 (26.4%), none in 2 (2.8%), not reported in 27 (37.5%) (Table 1, p. 2061).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; all 72 reports were appraised.
sample.selection_effects: Only two-arm parallel-group superiority trials with a clearly identified primary outcome and entirely non-significant primary results, from one month of 2006, in English: 72 of 616 trial reports (12%), mostly small trials in specialty journals. The authors note that spin may be more likely when results are non-significant, and that other strategies may exist in other trials (p. 2063).

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. Spin was identified by two readers (the first and second authors) independently with a pretested, standardized form, then by consensus or with a third reader (the last author); all authors developed the classification scheme from the literature, examples sent by members of the Cochrane Statistical Methods Group and a sample of trials with non-significant results (p. 2059).

comparison.controls: None. Abstracts and main texts of the same reports are compared descriptively.

outcomes.instruments: Spin by section (title; abstract Results and Conclusions; main-text Results, Discussion and Conclusions); by strategy (focus on significant within-group, secondary-outcome, subgroup or modified-population results; interpreting non-significant results as equivalence or comparable effectiveness; claiming or emphasizing benefit despite non-significance; other strategies recorded and classified later); extent (number of sections with spin); and level in Conclusions (high, moderate or low, by uncertainty in the framing, recommendations for further trials and acknowledgment of the non-significant primary result). Also recorded: whether abstracts identified the primary outcome and how results were reported (pp. 2059–2060).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validated measure of spin exists; the authors call the extent and level classifications exploratory, not validated and not a scoring system (p. 2060), and acknowledge subjectivity (pp. 2062–2063). Agreement between readers: κ = 0.47 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.67) for spin in abstract Conclusions and 0.64 (0.47 to 0.82) for spin in article Conclusions (p. 2059).
outcomes.operationalization: Spin: specific reporting strategies, from whatever motive, to highlight that the experimental treatment is beneficial despite a non-significant difference in the primary outcome, or to distract the reader from the non-significant results (p. 2059). Significance by P < .05; the authors note that trials should not be interpreted on the 0.05 threshold alone (p. 2063).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive proportions with 95% CIs for spin in six report sections (and its strategies), no hypothesis tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The readers knew that every included trial had a non-significant primary outcome (the selection criterion), and they were authors who had developed the scheme.

analysis.effect_sizes: Spin among 72 reports (95% CIs, reproduced as exact intervals by the editors): title 13 (18.0%; 10.0% to 28.9%); abstract Results 27 (37.5%; 26.4% to 49.7%); abstract Conclusions 42 (58.3%; 46.1% to 69.8%), 17 of them (23.6%; 14.4% to 35.1%) focusing only on treatment effectiveness; main-text Results 21 (29.2%; 19.0% to 41.1%), Discussion 31 (43.1%; 31.4% to 55.3%) and Conclusions 36 (50.0%; 38.0% to 62.0%). Spin in at least one section: 49 abstracts (68.1%; 56.0% to 78.6%) and 44 main texts (61.1%; 48.9% to 72.4%); in all sections 20 abstracts (27.8%; 17.9% to 39.6%) and 14 main texts (19.4%; 11.1% to 30.5%). High level of spin in Conclusions: 24 abstracts (33.3%; 22.7% to 45.4%) and 19 main texts (26.4%; 16.7% to 38.1%) (pp. 2058, 2060–2063; Tables 2 and 3). Reporting of the primary outcome: clearly identified in 44 abstracts (61.1%); a secondary outcome presented as primary in 3 (4.2%); effect size with 95% CI in only 9 abstracts (12.5%) and 16 main texts (22.2%); no number for the primary outcome in 28 abstracts (38.9%) (p. 2060). Editors' recalculation of the exact binomial intervals reproduces every interval checked except one typographical slip (reporting issues).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the classification scheme was developed by the authors before the appraisal (p. 2059).
analysis.selective_reporting: Every category is reported for all 72 reports (Tables 2 and 3); examples of spin are in online eTables 1 and 2 and an eAppendix, which were not among the files (pp. 2061, 2063).
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive). With 72 reports the main proportions carry intervals of about ±11 to 12 percentage points.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In these 72 reports more than half of abstract conclusions and half of main-text conclusions contained spin, a third of abstract conclusions at a high level; spin was more frequent in abstracts than in main texts; and few reports gave an effect size with a confidence interval for the primary outcome.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion, that in this representative sample of 2006 trials with non-significant primary outcomes reporting and interpretation were frequently inconsistent with the results (p. 2058), matches the data, with two qualifications: 'representative' describes the parent cohort of 616 reports, while the 72 analysed are a narrow subset (two-arm parallel-group trials with entirely non-significant primary outcomes); and spin rests on readers' judgement (κ 0.47 for abstract conclusions). The comment that the results are consistent with studies linking financial ties to favourable conclusions (p. 2061) has no analysis of spin by funding behind it in this study. The authors say plainly that they cannot tell whether spin was deliberate or whether it affected readers (p. 2063).

timeline.event: Earlier review cited by the authors: in 17 BMJ trial reports with non-significant results, the authors of 3 seemed to support the experimental intervention despite evidence that it might be ineffective (Hewitt et al., 2008, as summarized on p. 2063); not read

UK university health press releases: 33% to 40% stated advice, causal claims or human relevance more strongly than the journal article; the authors expect spin in the articles themselves to make their figures underestimates (pp. 3–4)

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no later study of spin in trial reports was read for this card. The authors call the work a first step and propose research on which categories and levels of spin affect readers' interpretation (p. 2064).

funding.funder: Dr Boutron was supported by a grant from the Societe Francaise de Rhumatologie (SFR) and the Lavoisier Program (Ministère des Affaires étrangères et européennes) (printed 'that Lavoisier Program'); the sponsors had no role in the design and conduct of the study, the data, or the preparation, review or approval of the manuscript (p. 2064).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Statistics in Medicine, University of Oxford, and INSERM U738, Hôpital Hôtel Dieu and Université Paris Descartes, Paris (p. 2058). The cohort of trial reports comes from an earlier study whose authors include two of this paper's authors (ref. 11: Hopewell, Dutton, Yu, Chan & Altman, 2010).

what_would_settle_it: Randomized experiments showing readers the same trial abstract with and without spin and measuring their judgement of benefit; and repeated, preregistered surveys of spin in larger and more recent samples of trials, including trials of drugs used outside medicine, with readers blind to journal and funding.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: A cohort of all PubMed-indexed RCT reports published in one month of 2006, described in an earlier study (pp. 2059–2060).
Every report in the cohort that met the criteria was included (72 of 205 parallel-group trials with identified primary outcomes) (Figure, p. 2060).
72 reports give the main proportions within about ±11 to 12 percentage points; individual strategies rest on 1 to 17 reports.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 describes journals, medical areas, outcomes, sample sizes, impact factors, citations, interventions, comparators and funding (p. 2061).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 72 reports appraised for every category (Tables 2 and 3, pp. 2062–2063).

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Spin is defined explicitly and classified with a scheme built from the literature and examples, but the scheme is not validated, and the extent and level classes are exploratory (pp. 2059–2060).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Two independent readers with a pretested form and consensus, but agreement was moderate (κ 0.47 for abstract conclusions, 0.64 for article conclusions; p. 2059); blinding to journal, authors or funding is not reported, and one reviewer classified significance at screening.
Proportions with 95% CIs (p. 2060; Tables 1–3), which the editors' recalculation reproduces as exact intervals; the paper does not name the method.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI items applied to a sample of published trial reports, as the round brief asks for studies of how research is reported. The frame is complete for one month of PubMed-indexed trials and the appraisal was done in duplicate with a standard form, so the counts are sound; the uncertainty lies in judging what counts as spin (moderate agreement, a scheme developed and applied by the same authors) and in the narrow subset (72 two-arm trials of 2006 with entirely non-significant primary outcomes). The source may be cited for how often, in such trials, abstracts and conclusions presented a non-significant primary result as a benefit, as equivalence or as proof of safety, or moved attention to significant secondary, subgroup or within-group results, and for spin being more frequent in abstracts than in main texts. It may not be cited for spin in trials with significant results or in other designs, for whether spin misleads readers, or for a link with industry funding.

key_findings.finding: Of 616 reports of randomized trials published in December 2006, 205 were two-arm parallel-group trials with a clearly identified primary outcome; of these, 124 had significant primary results, 9 unclear results, and 72 non-significant results for all primary outcomes, which were appraised.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Selection of Articles, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 2059); Figure (Study Selection) and Results › General Characteristics of Selected Articles, 1st paragraph (p. 2060)

key_findings.finding: Spin appeared in the title of 13 of 72 reports (18.0%; 95% CI 10.0% to 28.9%), in the abstract Results of 27 (37.5%; 26.4% to 49.7%) and in the abstract Conclusions of 42 (58.3%; 46.1% to 69.8%); 17 abstract Conclusions (23.6%; 14.4% to 35.1%) focused only on treatment effectiveness.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 2058); Results › Spin Strategies, 1st paragraph (p. 2060); Table 2 (p. 2062)
key_findings.note: Printed as 18.0% (editors' calculation: 13 of 72 is 18.06%; reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Spin appeared in the main-text Results of 21 reports (29.2%; 19.0% to 41.1%), the Discussion of 31 (43.1%; 31.4% to 55.3%) and the Conclusions of 36 (50.0%; 38.0% to 62.0%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Spin Strategies, 1st paragraph (starts p. 2060, ends p. 2061); Table 2 (p. 2062)

key_findings.finding: 49 abstracts (68.1%; 56.0% to 78.6%) and 44 main texts (61.1%; 48.9% to 72.4%) had spin in at least one section; 20 abstracts (27.8%; 17.9% to 39.6%) and 14 main texts (19.4%; 11.1% to 30.5%) in all sections; more than 40% of articles had spin in at least two main-text sections (editors' calculation from Table 3: 30 of 72, 41.7%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Extent of Spin, 1st paragraph (p. 2061); Table 3 (p. 2063)

key_findings.finding: The level of spin in Conclusions was high (no uncertainty in the framing, no call for further trials and no acknowledgment of the non-significant primary result, or a recommendation to use the treatment in clinical practice) in 24 abstracts (33.3%; 22.7% to 45.4%) and 19 main texts (26.4%; 16.7% to 38.1%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Level of Spin in Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 2061); Table 3 (p. 2063)

key_findings.finding: Strategies in abstract Conclusions: claiming equivalence or comparable effectiveness from non-significant results 10 (13.9%), claiming efficacy without regard to the non-significant primary outcome 4 (5.6%), focusing only on significant results 3 (4.2%); 9 (12.5%) acknowledged the non-significant primary outcome but emphasized benefit or other significant results; others ruled out adverse events from non-significant results (3, 4.2%), concluded from within-group change that both treatments worked (6, 8.3%) or recommended the treatment (3, 4.2%). In abstract Results, spin was mostly a focus on significant within-group comparisons (8, 11.1%) or subgroup analyses (6, 8.3%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Spin Strategies, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 2061); Table 2 (p. 2062)
key_findings.note: Strategy counts are not mutually exclusive in the main text: Discussion strategies add up to 33 for 31 reports and Conclusions strategies to 40 for 36 (Table 2, footnotes b–e, p. 2062).

key_findings.finding: The primary outcome was clearly identified in 44 of 72 abstracts (61.1%); 3 abstracts (4.2%) presented a secondary outcome as the primary one; only 9 abstracts (12.5%) gave the effect size with a 95% CI and 28 (38.9%) gave no number for the primary outcome; in the main text 16 reports (22.2%) gave the effect size with its precision and 21 (29.2%) only group summary statistics without precision.
key_findings.locator: Results › Reporting of Primary Outcomes in Abstract and Main Text, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Spin strategies described by the authors include reading P > .05 as showing a similar effect in trials not designed to test equivalence (used only against active comparators), treating within-group change as if the trial were a before-after study (a significant change in the experimental arm but not in the comparator taken as benefit), concluding lack of harm from non-significant safety results, and in one report comparing the experimental group with the placebo group of another trial.

Spin was more frequent in abstracts than in main texts, which the authors call important because readers often judge a trial from its freely available abstract and clinical decisions are sometimes made from the abstract alone.

As an example of a strategy outside their scheme, the authors cite the VIGOR report, which presented myocardial infarction risk as a protective effect of the comparator naproxen (relative risk 0.2; 95% CI 0.1 to 0.7) instead of harm from rofecoxib (relative risk 5.00; 95% CI 1.68 to 20.13).
key_findings.note: Figures from the cited reports (refs 37 and 38), not from this study's data.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that they cannot tell whether the spin was deliberately misleading, the result of lack of knowledge, or both, nor whether it affected peer reviewers' and readers' interpretations; they acknowledge that judging spin involved subjectivity and that trials should not be interpreted on the P = .05 threshold alone.
Agreement between the two readers was moderate: κ 0.47 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.67) for spin in abstract Conclusions and 0.64 (0.47 to 0.82) for spin in article Conclusions.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Assessment of Selected Articles, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 prints the 95% CI for the 7 of 72 abstracts with spin in one section other than the Conclusions as 0.4% to 19.0%; the same proportion has 4.0% to 19.0% elsewhere in the paper (Tables 1 and 2), and that is the exact interval for 7 of 72.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the count and percentage are correct.

reporting_issues.issue: 13 of 72 is printed as 18.0% in the abstract, the Results and Table 2 (editors' calculation: 18.06%, which rounds to 18.1%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible rounding slip; the interval printed (10.0% to 28.9%) is the exact interval for 13 of 72.

reporting_issues.issue: Diagnostic test accuracy reports were an exclusion criterion, yet Table 1 lists one included report whose primary outcome was diagnosis accuracy.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a randomized comparison of diagnostic strategies rather than an accuracy study; it concerns 1 of 72 reports.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment says the results are consistent with studies linking financial ties to favourable conclusions, but spin is not analysed by funding source in this study, and funding was not reported for 27 of the 72 trials (37.5%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The study gives no evidence on funding and spin; do not cite it for that.
